## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.91420.4.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.91420.4.sa1)

Gating of Kv10 channels is unique because it involves coupling between non-domain swapped voltage sensing domains, a domain-swapped cytoplasmic ring assembly formed by the N- and C-termini, and the pore domain. Recent structural data suggests that activation of the voltage sensing domain relieves a steric hindrance to pore opening, but the contribution of the cytoplasmic domain to gating is still not well understood. This aspect is of particular importance because proteins like calmodulin interact with the cytoplasmic domain to regulate channel activity. The effects of calmodulin (CaM) in WT and mutant channels with disrupted cytoplasmic gating ring assemblies are contradictory, resulting in inhibition or activation, respectively. The underlying mechanism for these discrepancies is not understood. In the present manuscript, Reham Abdelaziz and collaborators use electrophysiology, biochemistry and mathematical modeling to describe how mutations and deletions that disrupt inter-subunit interactions at the cytoplasmic gating ring assembly affect Kv10.1 channel gating and modulation by CaM. In the revised manuscript, additional information is provided to allow readers to identify within the Kv10.1 channel structure the location of E600R, one of the key channel mutants analyzed in this study. However, the mechanistic role of the cytoplasmic domains that this study focuses on, as well as the location of the ΔPASCap deletion and other perturbations investigated in the study remain difficult to visualize without additional graphical information.

The authors focused mainly on two structural perturbations that disrupt interactions within the cytoplasmic domain, the E600R mutant and the ΔPASCap deletion. By expressing mutants in oocytes and recording currents using Two Electrode Voltage-Clamp (TEV), it is found that both ΔPASCap and E600R mutants have biphasic conductance-voltage (G-V) relations and exhibit activation and deactivation kinetics with multiple voltage-dependent components. Importantly, the mutant-specific component in the G-V relations is observed at negative voltages where WT channels remain closed. The authors argue that the biphasic behavior in the G-V relations is unlikely to result from two different populations of channels in the oocytes, because they found that the relative amplitude between the two components in the G-V relations was highly reproducible across individual oocytes that otherwise tend to show high variability in expression levels. Instead, the G-V relations for all mutant channels could be well described by an equation that considers two open states O1 and O2, and a transition between them; O1 appeared to be unaffected by any of the structural manipulations tested (i.e. E600R, ΔPASCap, and other deletions) whereas the parameters for O2 and the transition between the two open states were different between constructs. The O1 state is not observed in WT channels and is hypothesized to be associated with voltage sensor activation. O2 represents the open state that is normally observed in WT channels and is speculated to be associated with conformational changes within the cytoplasmic gating ring that follow voltage sensor activation, which could explain why the mutations and deletions disrupting cytoplasmic interactions affect primarily O2.

Severing the covalent link between the voltage sensor and pore reduced O1 occupancy in one of the deletion constructs. Although this observation is consistent with the hypothesis that voltage-sensor activation drives entry into O1, this result is not conclusive. Structural as well as functional data has established that the coupling of the voltage sensor and pore does not entirely rely on the S4-S5 covalent linker between the sensor and the pore, and thus the severed construct could still retain coupling through other mechanisms, which is consistent with the prominent voltage dependence that is observed. If both states O1 and O2 require voltage sensor activation, it is unclear why the severed construct would affect state O1 primarily, as suggested in the manuscript, as opposed to decreasing occupancy of both open states. In line with this argument, the presence of Mg2+ in the extracellular solution affected both O1 and O2. This finding suggests that entry into both O1 and O2 requires voltage-sensor activation because Mg2+ ions are known to stabilize the voltage sensor in its most deactivated conformations.

Activation towards and closure from O1 is slow, whereas channels close rapidly from O2. A rapid alternating pulse protocol was used to take advantage of the difference in activation and deactivation kinetics between the two open components in the mutants and thus drive an increasing number of channels towards state O1. Currents activated by the alternating protocol reached larger amplitudes than those elicited by a long depolarization to the same voltage. This finding is interpreted as an indication that O1 has a larger macroscopic conductance than O2. In the revised manuscript, the authors performed single-channel recordings to determine why O1 and O2 have different macroscopic conductance. The results show that at voltages where the state O1 predominates, channels exhibited longer open times and overall higher open probability, whereas at more depolarized voltages where occupancy of O2 increases, channels exhibited more flickery gating behavior and decreased open probability. These results are informative but not conclusive since single-channel amplitudes could not be resolved at strong depolarizations, limiting the extent to which the data could be analyzed. In the last revision, the authors have included one representative example showing inhibition of single channel activity by the Kv10-specific inhibitor astemizole. Group data analysis would be needed to conclusively establish that the currents that were recorded indeed correspond to Kv10 channels.

It is shown that conditioning pulses to very negative voltages result in mutant channel currents that are larger and activate more slowly than those elicited at the same voltage but starting from less negative conditioning pulses. In voltage-activated curves, O1 occupancy is shown to be favored by increasingly negative conditioning voltages. This is interpreted as indicating that O1 is primarily accessed from deeply closed states in which voltage sensors are in their most deactivated position. Consistently, a mutation that destabilizes these deactivated states is shown to largely suppress the first component in voltage-activation curves for both ΔPASCap and E600R channels.

The authors then address the role of the hidden O1 state in channel regulation by calcium-calmodulin (CaM). Stimulating calcium entry into oocytes with ionomycin and thapsigargin, assumed to enhance CaM-dependent modulation, resulted in preferential potentiation of the first component in ΔPASCap and E600R channels. This potentiation was attenuated by including an additional mutation that disfavors deeply closed states. Together, these results are interpreted as an indication that calcium-CaM preferentially stabilizes deeply closed states from which O1 can be readily accessed in mutant channels, thus favoring current activation. In WT channels lacking a conducting O1 state, CaM stabilizes deeply closed states and is therefore inhibitory. It is found that the potentiation of ΔPASCap and E600R by CaM is more strongly attenuated by mutations in the channel that are assumed to disrupt interaction with the C-terminal lobe of CaM than mutations assumed to affect interaction with the N-terminal lobe. These results are intriguing but difficult to interpret in mechanistic terms. The strong effect that calcium-CaM had on the occupancy of the O1 state in the mutants raises the possibility that O1 can be only observed in channels that are constitutively associated with CaM. To address this, a biochemical pull-down assay was carried out to establish that only a small fraction of channels are associated with CaM under baseline conditions. These CaM experiments are potentially very interesting and could have wide physiological relevance. However, the approach utilized to activate CaM is indirect and could result in additional non-specific effects on the oocytes that could affect the results.

Finally, a mathematical model is proposed consisting of two layers involving two activation steps for the voltage sensor, and one conformational change in the cytoplasmic gating ring - completion of both sets of conformational changes is required to access state O2, but accessing state O1 only requires completion of the first voltage-sensor activation step in the four subunits. The model qualitatively reproduces most major findings on the mutants. Although the model used is highly symmetric and appears simple, the mathematical form used for the rate constants in the model adds a layer of complexity to the model that makes mechanistic interpretations difficult. In addition, many transitions that from a mechanistic standpoint should not depend on voltage were assigned a voltage dependence in the model. These limitations diminish the mechanistic insight that can be reliably extracted from the model.

claims.source: Since they allow dissection of the ring-dependent effect, our mutants will allow for a direct study of such modulation mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the mutants for future studies.

results.result: The study identifies a novel open state (O1) in KV10.1 mutants with disrupted intracellular ring interactions that differs from the wild-type open state (O2) and can explain previously unexplained mutant behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C62, and C207 collectively establish the central finding that mutants with altered PASCap-CNBHD interactions reveal a distinct open state. This is supported by comprehensive electrophysiological data (Figures 1-2), single-channel recordings (Figure 5), and mathematical modeling (Figure 9) that consistently demonstrate two kinetically distinct open states with different conductance properties.

results.result: ΔPASCap and E600R mutants exhibit hyperpolarized activation thresholds and biphasic conductance-voltage relationships, contrasting with wild-type channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 and C86-C89 describe the shifted activation threshold and biphasic GV curves directly observed in Figure 1B. The data show consistent, reproducible biphasic behavior across multiple mutants with quantified voltage shifts (−80 mV vs. −40 mV for WT), providing strong experimental support.

results.result: Global fitting analysis reveals that the first component of the biphasic GV is conserved across all N-terminal deletion mutants, while the second component shifts with increasing deletion size.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C99 describe the global fitting results shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1. The mathematical analysis using Equation 3b successfully describes all mutant GV curves with shared parameters for the first component, providing quantitative support for two distinct gating processes.

results.result: The biphasic gating behavior reflects two sequential steps: voltage sensor movement leading to a pre-open state (O1, conducting in mutants but not WT), followed by ring reconfiguration leading to the conventional open state (O2).
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 present the mechanistic interpretation of the biphasic behavior. This is well-supported by the global fit analysis (Figure 2), the split channel experiments (C103-C105), and Mg2+ experiments (C108-C111) that demonstrate voltage sensor involvement in both components while the ring transition is unaffected by extracellular divalents.

results.result: Single-channel recordings of ΔPASCap reveal two kinetically distinct classes of openings: long-lasting openings (hundreds of milliseconds) at weak depolarizations and brief openings at strong depolarizations, with transitions between them requiring closed intermediate states.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C130 and C236 describe single-channel data shown in Figure 5. The recordings provide direct evidence for two open states with voltage-dependent kinetics, and the observation that transitions between them require closed intermediates supports the model structure. Control experiments with astemizole (C125) confirm channel identity.

results.result: The mutant-specific open state O1 lacks the rapid flicker block characteristic of O2, resulting in larger macroscopic currents due to higher open probability.
results.evaluation: Claims C63, C64, and C217 explain the mechanism underlying larger currents in O1. This is supported by single-channel recordings showing distinct kinetic behaviors (Figure 5) and modeling results (Figure 9) that require a flicker block for O2 but not O1 to reproduce experimental observations.

results.result: Alternating brief depolarizing and hyperpolarizing pulses cause current accumulation in mutants that exceeds sustained depolarization, consistent with preferential accumulation in the slowly-deactivating O1 state.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C121 describe the alternating pulse experiments shown in Figure 4. The observation that intermittent stimulation produces larger currents than sustained depolarization in mutants but not WT provides strong functional evidence for a slowly-deactivating open state (O1) that accumulates during the protocol.

results.result: Hyperpolarizing prepulses potentiate the first component of the biphasic response in mutants but not WT, indicating that O1 is preferentially accessed from deep closed states.
results.evaluation: Claims C65 and C135-C142 describe prepulse experiments shown in Figures 6-7. The data demonstrate that −160 mV prepulses increase current amplitude by 3-4 fold in mutants with no effect in WT, and specifically potentiate the first GV component. This provides strong evidence that O1 is accessed from hyperpolarized closed states.

results.result: The L322H mutation, which restricts access to deep closed states, dramatically attenuates the first component of the biphasic GV in both ΔPASCap and E600R backgrounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C147 describe experiments shown in Figure 7C-D. The L322H mutation, known from prior work (C143) to limit deep closed states, eliminates the biphasic behavior and rectification in mutant backgrounds, providing strong genetic evidence linking deep closed states to O1 accessibility.

results.result: Elevated intracellular Ca2+ paradoxically increases current amplitude in mutants by promoting access to O1, converting the biphasic IV relationship to a linear one, with effects reversing as Ca2+ levels decline.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 and C151-C177 describe Ca2+ experiments shown in Figure 8. The data demonstrate that Ca2+ elevation causes transient linearization of the IV curve and current potentiation in mutants, with time courses matching Ca2+ dynamics (Figure 8—supplement 1). This explains the previously paradoxical Ca2+ effects in these mutants.

results.result: Ca2+-CaM restores biphasic behavior in L322H mutants that normally show reduced access to deep closed states, supporting the hypothesis that Ca2+-CaM drives channels into deep closed states.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C164 and C226 describe experiments shown in Figure 8A-B (upper right panels). The observation that Ca2+ induces biphasic behavior in L322H mutants that lack it at baseline provides strong mechanistic evidence that Ca2+-CaM promotes deep closed state occupancy, thereby facilitating O1 access.

results.result: Mutation of the C-terminal CaM binding site (BDC2) eliminates or attenuates the first component of the biphasic GV, with stronger effects in ΔPASCap than E600R.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C169 describe experiments shown in Figure 8C-D. The differential effects of BDC2 mutations in the two mutant backgrounds provide evidence for CaM's role in stabilizing O1, though the incomplete effect in E600R suggests mutant-specific differences in CaM dependence.

results.result: A two-layer Markov model with two open states (O1 and O2), three gating steps (two VSD movements and ring rotation), and a flicker block for O2 successfully reproduces all key experimental observations including biphasic GV curves, complex tail kinetics, prepulse effects, and alternating pulse responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C68 and C182-C237 describe the mathematical model shown in Figure 9 and supplements. The model quantitatively reproduces biphasic activation, triphasic tail currents, prepulse-dependent potentiation, alternating pulse accumulation, and Ca2+ effects. While the authors acknowledge limitations (C180, C247), the model successfully captures all major experimental features.

results.result: The split channel Δ2-10.L341Split shows reduced first component compared to Δ2-10, indicating that coupling of voltage sensor motion to O1 entry does not require a continuous S4-S5 linker but suggests a downstream mechanism beyond position 342.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 describe the split channel experiment shown in Figure 2C-D. The data demonstrate that severing the S4-S5 linker reduces but does not eliminate O1 access, providing important mechanistic insight into voltage sensor coupling. However, the interpretation of the downstream mechanism (C105) is somewhat speculative.

results.result: Extracellular Mg2+ slows activation and shifts voltage dependence for both gating components but does not affect the transition between them, consistent with Mg2+ affecting voltage sensor movement while the ring transition occurs in the cytoplasm.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 and C216 describe Mg2+ experiments shown in Figure 3. The data show that Mg2+ affects both GV components equally (~25 mV shift) but not the transition voltage between them, supporting the model that both components involve voltage sensor movement while the inter-component transition reflects cytoplasmic ring reconfiguration.

results.result: Mutant channels show dramatically altered activation and deactivation kinetics compared to WT, with voltage-dependent transitions between slow monotonic deactivation (weak depolarizations) and fast biphasic deactivation (strong depolarizations).
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C85 describe kinetic data shown in Figures 1C-F. The detailed characterization of voltage-dependent kinetic changes provides strong evidence for state-dependent gating, with quantitative measurements showing mutants activate much slower at weak depolarizations but reach WT speeds at strong depolarizations.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that O1 corresponds to the 'non-conducting state 2' identified in KV10.2 by cryo-EM, where an intact intracellular ring prevents ion flow in WT but ring disruption in mutants allows permeation.
results.evaluation: Claims C208-C209 present a structural hypothesis linking O1 to a specific cryo-EM structure. While this is a reasonable hypothesis based on structural similarity between KV10.1 and KV10.2 (C47), it remains speculative without direct structural evidence. The hypothesis is plausible but requires validation through structural studies of the mutants.

results.result: The biphasic behavior is unlikely to result from two independent channel populations because mutant behavior is highly reproducible despite variable basal Ca2+ levels in oocytes, and only a small fraction (~4%) of channels are CaM-bound at basal Ca2+.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C176 and C210-C211 present arguments against the two-population hypothesis. The consistency of mutant behavior across oocytes (C170), the inability of two populations to explain voltage-dependent transitions (C172), astemizole block of single-channel activity (C211), and pull-down data showing low basal CaM binding (C173-C176) collectively provide strong evidence against this alternative explanation.

results.result: The study explains the mechanism of gating inhibition by Ca2+-Calmodulin: Ca2+-CaM stabilizes deep closed states, which inhibits WT channels (lacking permeable O1) but paradoxically activates mutants by promoting access to the high-conductance O1 state.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C177, C225, and C227 present the mechanistic explanation for Ca2+-CaM effects. This is well-supported by the Ca2+ experiments (Figure 8), L322H rescue experiments (C226), and the logical consistency of the mechanism with all observations. The explanation resolves the previously paradoxical Ca2+ effects in mutants.

results.result: The presented model structure is among the simplest that can reproduce the data, with fundamental features (three gating steps, flicker block, O1/O2 separation) being necessary, though finer structural details remain uncertain and the model never fits all experiments perfectly.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C181 and C245-C253 provide an honest assessment of model limitations. The authors acknowledge that while the fundamental structure is well-constrained by data (C245-C246), finer details are uncertain (C247), automated global fitting was difficult (C181), and perfect fits were not achieved (C180). This transparent discussion of limitations is appropriate and does not undermine the model's explanatory power.

results.result: Ca2+ effects in the model are implemented by shifting the voltage dependence of two transitions (γ↔δ and κ), which increases occupancy of the lower layer states and thereby access to O1.
results.evaluation: Claims C197-C198 and C188-C189 describe how Ca2+ effects are modeled (Figure 9D-E). The approach of shifting activation energies to represent Ca2+-CaM binding effects is mechanistically reasonable and successfully reproduces the experimental observations of linearized IV curves at high Ca2+.

results.result: The WT model is derived from the mutant model by removing O1 access and shifting ring rotation parameters in the hyperpolarizing direction to reflect more stable intracellular domain interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C200-C201 describe the WT model adaptation. This approach is logical and parsimonious, requiring minimal parameter changes to account for the structural differences between WT and mutants. The model successfully reproduces WT prepulse-dependent kinetics (C201).

results.result: E600R-specific features (transient current peak, larger tail currents) can be reproduced by reducing the O2→C2 rate constant and increasing the C2/O2 occupancy ratio, and the model can mimic KV11.1 with further parameter adjustments.
results.evaluation: Claims C202-C205 describe E600R-specific modeling shown in Figure 9—supplement 5. The ability to reproduce E600R features and even mimic KV11.1 behavior with parameter adjustments demonstrates the model's flexibility and suggests mechanistic similarities across KCNH family members.

results.result: The initial hypothesis that CaM participates constitutively in gating is unlikely correct based on low basal CaM binding; instead, effects of CaM binding site mutations may relate more to their protein location than CaM binding ability.
results.evaluation: Claims C228-C229 represent a revision of the authors' initial hypothesis based on pull-down data (Figure 8—supplement 4). This honest reassessment is scientifically appropriate, though the alternative explanation (C229) remains speculative and would benefit from additional structural or functional data.

results.result: Background on KCNH channel structure, function, and gating mechanisms, including differences from Shaker-type channels and the role of intracellular domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C29 provide established background knowledge about KCNH channels, supported by extensive citations. These claims establish the scientific context and rationale for the study, describing known structural features, gating differences from other K+ channel families, and the importance of intracellular domains.

results.result: Background on the intracellular ring structure, its role in gating, CaM binding sites and effects, and current gaps in understanding of voltage sensor-ring coupling.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C57 provide additional background on intracellular domain structure and function, CaM binding and effects, and identify gaps in current understanding. These are well-supported by citations and establish the specific questions addressed by the study, particularly the mechanism of voltage sensor-ring coupling.

results.result: Background on the Cole-Moore shift in KV10.1, its relationship to deep closed states, and its compromise by N-terminal deletions.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C134 provide background on the Cole-Moore shift, a well-established feature of KV10.1 gating. This background is important for interpreting the prepulse experiments and is well-supported by citations.

results.result: No cumulative inactivation was detected in any mutants after repeated depolarization.
results.evaluation: Claim C141 reports a negative result that is important for interpretation. The absence of cumulative inactivation (demonstrated in Figure 4) supports the interpretation that current changes reflect state transitions rather than inactivation processes.

results.result: Changes in tail current amplitude likely reflect true changes in overall conductance rather than artifacts.
results.evaluation: Claim C90 provides an interpretation of tail current data based on correlation with conductance measurements. This is a reasonable inference supported by the consistency between tail amplitude changes and GV measurements (Figure 1B).

results.result: Similar biphasic behavior has been mentioned for other mutations affecting intracellular domains, but the reasons have not been previously investigated.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 place the current findings in context of prior observations. The citations support that biphasic behavior has been noted before, and C92 correctly identifies that mechanistic investigation was lacking, establishing the novelty of the current study.

results.result: Background on the effects of extracellular divalent cations on KV10.1 activation kinetics and their correlation with hydration enthalpy.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 provide background on divalent cation effects, well-supported by citations. This background is essential for interpreting the Mg2+ experiments and their implications for voltage sensor movement.

results.result: Single-channel activity was never detected in uninjected oocytes and was silenced by astemizole, confirming it results from ΔPASCap expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C125 describe essential control experiments for single-channel recordings. The negative control (uninjected oocytes) and pharmacological validation (astemizole block, Figure 5—supplement 1) provide strong evidence that observed activity is channel-specific.

results.result: Background on Ca2+-CaM effects: inhibition of WT channels is well-established, while paradoxical potentiation in mutants has been reported.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C150 provide background on Ca2+-CaM effects, establishing the paradox that the study aims to explain. The claims are well-supported by citations and set up the rationale for the Ca2+ experiments.

results.result: The presence of a second open state with larger openings when ring integrity is compromised could explain larger currents in heteromeric KV11.1 channels and may have physiological relevance.
results.evaluation: Claims C218-C219 speculate about physiological relevance to heteromeric KV11.1 channels. While this is an interesting hypothesis supported by citation of relevant work on HERG1a/1b channels, it remains speculative without direct experimental evidence in the heteromeric context.

results.result: Summary and implications: KV10.1 gating involves sequential voltage sensor movement (permissive) and ring rotation (effective gate opening), with implications for modulation and physiological function.
results.evaluation: Claims C230-C260 provide summary statements and discuss implications. These are well-supported by the cumulative evidence from the study and appropriately discuss the significance for understanding KCNH channel regulation and function.

results.result: Summary of the study's approach and model structure: two open states, three gating steps (two VSD, one ring), with O1 accessible after first VSD displacement and O2 requiring complete VSD displacement and ring reconfiguration.
results.evaluation: Claims C235-C244 summarize the study's main findings and model structure. These summary statements accurately reflect the experimental evidence and modeling results presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: Discussion of model complexity: sigmoidal voltage dependences point to more complicated underlying structure, and complex voltage dependence of κ signals unresolved structural details.
results.evaluation: Claims C248-C252 provide thoughtful discussion of model limitations and the relationship between model complexity and underlying biology. This honest assessment of what the model does and doesn't explain is scientifically appropriate.

results.result: The authors report that ΔPASCap and E600R mutants exhibit biphasic conductance-voltage (G-V) relationships with a hyperpolarizing shift in activation threshold compared to WT. The biphasic behavior can be described by an equation with two components (O1 and O2) and a transition between them, with the first component conserved across mutants and the second component varying with the extent of N-terminal deletions or ring disruption.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge that 'both ΔPASCap and E600R mutants have biphasic conductance-voltage (G-V) relations' and that 'the G-V relations for all mutant channels could be well described by an equation that considers two open states O1 and O2, and a transition between them.' The reviewers accept that O1 is 'unaffected by any of the structural manipulations tested' while O2 parameters differ between constructs.

results.result: The mutants display distinct activation and deactivation kinetics compared to WT, with slower activation at weak depolarizations that becomes similar to WT at strong depolarizations. Tail currents show complex voltage-dependent kinetics with slow deactivation after weak stimuli and fast deactivation after strong stimuli.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note that 'Activation towards and closure from O1 is slow, whereas channels close rapidly from O2' and describe the experimental observations showing 'the difference in activation and deactivation kinetics between the two open components in the mutants.' These kinetic differences are accepted as evidence for distinct open states.

results.result: The authors propose that gating involves two sequential steps: the first involves voltage sensor movement leading to a pre-open state (O1) that is non-conducting in WT but conducting in mutants, and the second involves ring reconfiguration leading to an open state (O2) in both WT and mutants.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this interpretation, stating 'O1 appeared to be unaffected by any of the structural manipulations tested...whereas the parameters for O2 and the transition between the two open states were different between constructs. The O1 state is not observed in WT channels and is hypothesized to be associated with voltage sensor activation. O2 represents the open state that is normally observed in WT channels and is speculated to be associated with conformational changes within the cytoplasmic gating ring.'

results.result: Severing the S4-S5 linker (Δ2-10.L341Split) reduced O1 occupancy, suggesting that coupling of voltage sensor motion to O2 entry does not require a continuous S4-S5 linker, but there is a mechanism downstream of S4 that conveys sensor motion to the gate.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note this result is 'consistent with the hypothesis that voltage-sensor activation drives entry into O1' but state 'this result is not conclusive.' They point out that 'the coupling of the voltage sensor and pore does not entirely rely on the S4-S5 covalent linker' and question 'why the severed construct would affect state O1 primarily...as opposed to decreasing occupancy of both open states.'

results.result: Extracellular Mg2+ slows activation of both open states and shifts voltage dependence, but does not affect the transition between O1 and O2, suggesting both states require voltage sensor activation and the transition occurs in the cytoplasm.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note that 'the presence of Mg2+ in the extracellular solution affected both O1 and O2. This finding suggests that entry into both O1 and O2 requires voltage-sensor activation because Mg2+ ions are known to stabilize the voltage sensor in its most deactivated conformations.' This observation raises questions about the interpretation that O1 is primarily associated with voltage sensor activation while O2 requires additional ring movement.

results.result: Rapid alternating pulse protocols drive accumulation of channels in O1, resulting in larger current amplitudes than sustained depolarizations. This is interpreted as evidence that O1 has larger macroscopic conductance than O2 due to slower deactivation kinetics.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe this protocol and accept the interpretation: 'A rapid alternating pulse protocol was used to take advantage of the difference in activation and deactivation kinetics between the two open components in the mutants and thus drive an increasing number of channels towards state O1. Currents activated by the alternating protocol reached larger amplitudes than those elicited by a long depolarization to the same voltage. This finding is interpreted as an indication that O1 has a larger macroscopic conductance than O2.'

results.result: Single-channel recordings from ΔPASCap show two classes of openings: long openings (hundreds of milliseconds) at weak depolarizations and shorter, flickery openings at strong depolarizations. Transitions between the two classes involve intermediate closed states, indicating no direct connection between the two open states.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the single-channel data but express reservations: 'The results show that at voltages where the state O1 predominates, channels exhibited longer open times and overall higher open probability, whereas at more depolarized voltages where occupancy of O2 increases, channels exhibited more flickery gating behavior and decreased open probability. These results are informative but not conclusive since single-channel amplitudes could not be resolved at strong depolarizations, limiting the extent to which the data could be analyzed.' They also note that 'Group data analysis would be needed to conclusively establish that the currents that were recorded indeed correspond to Kv10 channels.'

results.result: Hyperpolarizing prepulses increase current amplitude and slow activation kinetics in mutants but not in WT. The effect is stronger from -160 mV than -100 mV prepulses, potentiating the first component of the biphasic I-V relationship.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe these findings: 'It is shown that conditioning pulses to very negative voltages result in mutant channel currents that are larger and activate more slowly than those elicited at the same voltage but starting from less negative conditioning pulses. In voltage-activated curves, O1 occupancy is shown to be favored by increasingly negative conditioning voltages. This is interpreted as indicating that O1 is primarily accessed from deeply closed states in which voltage sensors are in their most deactivated position.'

results.result: The L322H mutation, which limits access to deep closed states in WT, drastically attenuates the first component of the biphasic G-V in both ΔPASCap and E600R mutants, with tail currents showing homogeneous kinetics, indicating reduced O1 occupancy.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state: 'Consistently, a mutation that destabilizes these deactivated states is shown to largely suppress the first component in voltage-activation curves for both ΔPASCap and E600R channels.' This result is accepted as supporting the hypothesis that O1 is accessed from deep closed states.

results.result: Elevating intracellular Ca2+ with ionomycin and thapsigargin potentiates the first component of the biphasic I-V in ΔPASCap and E600R mutants, making the response linear. This effect is transient and reversible. Ca2+-CaM binding is proposed to stabilize deep closed states from which O1 is accessed. Disrupting the C-terminal CaM binding site attenuates this effect.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the experiments but express concerns: 'Stimulating calcium entry into oocytes with ionomycin and thapsigargin, assumed to enhance CaM-dependent modulation, resulted in preferential potentiation of the first component in ΔPASCap and E600R channels.' However, they note significant limitations: 'These CaM experiments are potentially very interesting and could have wide physiological relevance. However, the approach utilized to activate CaM is indirect and could result in additional non-specific effects on the oocytes that could affect the results.' They also question whether O1 requires constitutive CaM association based on the pull-down data showing only a small fraction of channels bound to CaM at baseline.

results.result: Pull-down assays show that only a small fraction of channels (~4% at 100 nM Ca2+) are bound to CaM at basal Ca2+ levels, with dramatic increases at 0.5-1 μM Ca2+. This fraction is insufficient to explain the consistent biphasic behavior observed in mutants.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this biochemical data: 'To address this, a biochemical pull-down assay was carried out to establish that only a small fraction of channels are associated with CaM under baseline conditions.' This result is used to argue against constitutive CaM involvement in the biphasic phenotype, though reviewers note it raises questions about the mechanism of CaM's effects.

results.result: A Markov model with two layers (representing two voltage sensor activation steps) and one ring reconfiguration step reproduces key experimental observations including biphasic G-V, complex tail kinetics, prepulse effects, alternating pulse behavior, and Ca2+ effects. The model requires two open states (O1 and O2) with O2 subject to rapid flicker block.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the model reproduces major findings: 'a mathematical model is proposed...The model qualitatively reproduces most major findings on the mutants.' However, they express significant concerns about its mechanistic interpretation: 'Although the model used is highly symmetric and appears simple, the mathematical form used for the rate constants in the model adds a layer of complexity to the model that makes mechanistic interpretations difficult. In addition, many transitions that from a mechanistic standpoint should not depend on voltage were assigned a voltage dependence in the model. These limitations diminish the mechanistic insight that can be reliably extracted from the model.'

results.result: The observations are explained by coexistence of two open states: O1 (corresponding to a pre-open state in WT, possibly the 'non-conducting state 2' in KV10.2) made conducting by ring disruption, and O2 (the normal WT open state). Two independent channel populations are ruled out based on reproducibility and inability to explain voltage-dependent transitions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the two-state interpretation and the argument against two populations: 'The authors argue that the biphasic behavior in the G-V relations is unlikely to result from two different populations of channels in the oocytes, because they found that the relative amplitude between the two components in the G-V relations was highly reproducible across individual oocytes that otherwise tend to show high variability in expression levels.' The structural hypothesis about correspondence to KV10.2 states is noted but not critically evaluated.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the biphasic G-V curves and shifted activation thresholds (C69-C71, C87-C89, C93-C99). OpenEval finds strong support from Figure 1B data and global fitting. Peer reviewers explicitly accept the biphasic behavior and two-open-state interpretation, noting O1 is 'unaffected by structural manipulations' while O2 parameters differ between constructs.

Both address global fitting results (C93-C99). OpenEval emphasizes quantitative support from shared parameters in Equation 3b. Peer reviewers accept that 'G-V relations for all mutant channels could be well described by an equation that considers two open states O1 and O2.'

Perfect claim overlap (C100-C102) on mechanistic interpretation of biphasic behavior. OpenEval finds strong support from multiple experimental approaches. Peer reviewers accept the interpretation that O1 is associated with voltage sensor activation while O2 involves cytoplasmic ring changes, though they note both states require voltage sensor movement based on Mg2+ data.

Perfect claim overlap (C103-C105) on split channel experiments. OpenEval finds support but notes speculative interpretation of downstream mechanism. Peer reviewers state the result is 'consistent with the hypothesis' but 'not conclusive,' questioning why severing would affect O1 primarily rather than both open states.

High claim overlap (C108-C111) on Mg2+ experiments. OpenEval interprets equal Mg2+ shifts as supporting voltage sensor involvement in both components. Peer reviewers note this finding 'raises questions' about the interpretation that O1 is primarily voltage sensor-associated while O2 requires additional ring movement.

Perfect claim overlap (C112-C121) on alternating pulse experiments. Both find strong support. OpenEval emphasizes functional evidence for slowly-deactivating O1. Peer reviewers accept the interpretation that larger currents with alternating pulses indicate 'O1 has a larger macroscopic conductance than O2.'

High claim overlap (C122-C130, C236) on single-channel data. OpenEval finds support for two open states with voltage-dependent kinetics. Peer reviewers acknowledge the data as 'informative but not conclusive,' noting single-channel amplitudes couldn't be resolved at strong depolarizations and requesting group data analysis for definitive channel identification.

High claim overlap (C135-C142) on prepulse experiments. Both find strong support. OpenEval emphasizes 3-4 fold current potentiation demonstrating O1 access from hyperpolarized states. Peer reviewers accept that 'O1 occupancy is favored by increasingly negative conditioning voltages,' interpreting this as O1 being 'primarily accessed from deeply closed states.'

Perfect claim overlap (C143-C147) on L322H mutation effects. Both find strong support. OpenEval emphasizes genetic evidence linking deep closed states to O1 accessibility. Peer reviewers explicitly state the mutation 'largely suppress[es] the first component,' consistently supporting the hypothesis.

Partial claim overlap on Ca2+ experiments (C151, C154-C156, C177, C224). OpenEval finds strong support for Ca2+-CaM promoting deep closed state occupancy. Peer reviewers acknowledge the experiments as 'potentially very interesting' but express concerns about indirect activation approach causing 'non-specific effects on oocytes.'

Partial claim overlap (C162-C164, C226) on Ca2+ effects in L322H mutants. OpenEval finds strong mechanistic evidence that Ca2+-CaM promotes deep closed states. Peer reviewers note the experiments but question whether O1 requires constitutive CaM association based on pull-down data.

Minimal claim overlap (C166-C168) on BDC2 mutation effects. OpenEval finds support for CaM's role in stabilizing O1 but notes incomplete effects. Peer reviewers group this with broader Ca2+ experiments and express concerns about indirect manipulation approach.

Partial claim overlap (C173-C176) on pull-down data. Both accept the biochemical evidence showing low basal CaM binding. OpenEval uses this to argue against two-population hypothesis. Peer reviewers accept the data but note it raises questions about CaM's mechanism of action.

Minimal claim overlap (C228) on revised hypothesis. OpenEval notes appropriate scientific reassessment based on pull-down data. Peer reviewers accept the pull-down results showing only small fraction of channels bound to CaM at baseline.

Substantial claim overlap (C68, C182-C183, C190-C191, C194-C196, C199, C237) on mathematical modeling. OpenEval finds the model successfully captures all major experimental features despite acknowledged limitations. Peer reviewers state the model 'qualitatively reproduces most major findings' but express significant concerns that 'many transitions that from a mechanistic standpoint should not depend on voltage were assigned voltage dependence,' diminishing mechanistic insight.

Partial claim overlap (C178-C181) on model limitations. OpenEval commends transparent discussion of limitations without undermining explanatory power. Peer reviewers emphasize that 'the mathematical form used for rate constants adds a layer of complexity that makes mechanistic interpretations difficult.'

Partial claim overlap (C208-C209) on structural hypothesis. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the hypothesis is plausible but speculative without direct structural evidence. Peer reviewers note the structural correspondence to KV10.2 states but do not critically evaluate this hypothesis.

Partial claim overlap (C210-C211) on arguments against two-population hypothesis. OpenEval finds strong evidence from consistency across oocytes and astemizole block. Peer reviewers accept the argument, stating 'the relative amplitude between the two components was highly reproducible across individual oocytes.'

High claim overlap (C72-C85) on kinetic characterization. Both find strong support. OpenEval emphasizes voltage-dependent kinetic changes as evidence for state-dependent gating. Peer reviewers accept that 'Activation towards and closure from O1 is slow, whereas channels close rapidly from O2.'

Minimal claim overlap (C62) but both address central finding. OpenEval emphasizes comprehensive evidence from electrophysiology, single-channel recordings, and modeling for two kinetically distinct open states. Peer reviewers accept the biphasic G-V relations and two-open-state interpretation.

Minimal claim overlap (C63-C64) on mechanism of larger O1 currents. OpenEval finds support from single-channel and modeling data requiring flicker block for O2. Peer reviewers accept biphasic behavior but do not specifically evaluate the flicker block mechanism.

Minimal claim overlap (C177) on Ca2+-CaM mechanistic explanation. OpenEval finds strong support for mechanism resolving paradoxical Ca2+ effects. Peer reviewers acknowledge Ca2+ experiments but express concerns about indirect manipulation approach.
OpenEval evaluates Ca2+ modeling approach (C197-C198, C188-C189) as mechanistically reasonable and successful. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

Minimal claim overlap (C201) on WT model adaptation. OpenEval finds the approach logical and parsimonious. Peer reviewers mention the model but focus criticism on voltage dependence assignments rather than WT adaptation specifically.
OpenEval evaluates E600R-specific modeling (C202-C205) as demonstrating model flexibility and mechanistic similarities across KCNH family. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval evaluates extensive background claims (C1-C29) on KCNH channel structure and function as well-supported by citations. Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate background claims.
